items.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 9, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

Or you have all other kinds of folks, one of the graduates from North Texas, one of the funkiest drummers in the world, Mr. Rick Latham, wrote an entire, a number of manuals about funk drumming. You’ve got brush work, Clayton Cameron, the great Clayton Cameron on brushes. You’ve got Ed Thigpen on brushes. You’ve got all sorts of wonderful manuals and drum methods now that are workable and usable, and they’re written by people who actually can play that. But it’s going…

Right. Now I’m going to take a pause for a moment because my connection here needs to go from — I think I need to plug in my — Okay we’re back. So the student that comes in and plays — the first thing they show you is the recreation of a Steve Smith drum solo or a Butch Miles drum solo, and you say, “Very impressive. And now —”

Well the way the I like to try to teach my students with using some of these various methods is that I’ll teach them the methods themselves, the techniques that are in there. Because I’m a big believer in muscle memory, especially with drummers. If you play something and practice something over and over and over and over and over, you know exactly what I mean, sooner or later, believe it or not folks, the muscles will start to retain the memory of the motion that you’re making.
